newsitem.title: UK: Brazil seen failing to meet growth potential.
newsitem.headline: Brazil seen failing to meet growth potential.

text.p: The Brazilian economy is failing to meet its full potential for growth despite efforts to implement reforms that would ease the strain of its weighty trade and budget deficits, economists said on Monday.

But a consensus was forming around the notion that the country's stock market at least was headed for a positive six months, according to Neil Dougall, Latin America economist at Kleinwort Benson in London.
"As a result of its unresolved structural problems, the country is being obliged to accept an economic growth path well below long-run potential," he said.

"The twin deficits (fiscal and current account) will place a firm limit on Brazil's growth possibilities over the next few years -- unless the process of structural reform is dramatically speeded up."
Brazil's 4.1 percent overall Gross Domestic Product growth during 1995 is forecast to slip to 3.5 percent this year.

While the country's inflation-adjusted budget deficit is likely to end the year close to 4.0 percent of GDP -- almost double the government's forecast -- the main disappointment is coming from its export scenario, Dougall said.
Official forecasts of a $2 billion trade surplus for 1996 look wildly optimistic, with a $3.5 billion deficit now more likely, he said.
"After growing by over 16 percent year-on-year in the first two months of this year, the pace of export expansion slowed to less than 2.0 percent in the third quarter," he said.
"In daily average terms..., the year-on-year growth in exports has now turned negative."

While an overvalued exchange rate may appear the main culprit, Dougall said the Brazilian Real was only overvalued by about 5.0 percent in purchasing power parity terms. A strong exchange rate did not necessarily impede growth, as Argentina's export story this year showed, he said.
"The contrast so far this year is...stark: a 22 percent growth in Argentina's exports compared with just 5.0 percent in Brazil," he said.

Brazil's central bank was almost certain to shrug off increasing calls to depreciate the Real until the country's fiscal situation improved, he said, owing to the bank's reliance on the exchange rate anchor to stifle inflation.
While some analysts are talking of a trade deficit of up to $8.0 billion in 1997, Dougall said this looked over-pessimistic.
"Instead, it is more likely that the authorities will be forced to aim for a lower economic growth trajectory," he said.

Stephen Rose, of Latin American brokerage Stephen Rose and Partners, agreed that structural problems still dragged heavily on economic growth. But he foresaw stock market strength looking ahead to April 1997.

"We...continue to look for a good market through at least the first quarter of next year, based principally on the belief that (President Fernando Henrique) Cardoso will be president for the next six years and that (this) will allow him to make genuine progress with the structural problems that still hold back Brazilian economic growth," he said.

Cardoso is seeking a constitutional change that would let him stand for a second term in office, and Rose predicted the president was likely to muster the requisite votes between now and January next year.

He based his stock market outlook on a series of forecasts, including Cardoso's re-election once the amendment is passed, and the likelihood of his mustering a stable political coalition to support reforms.

"My only trouble with our overall conclusion that the next six months will be good for Brazil and for the Brazilian stock market is that this is rapidly becoming the consensus view," Rose said. -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 2734
